questions.q: How is the absolute refractive index (n) of a transparent medium defined, and what value range does it take?
options: The speed of light in the medium divided by the speed of light in a vacuum; always less than 1
The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum (c) to the speed of light in the medium (v); always larger than 1
The product of the incident angle and the refracted angle; always equal to 1
The frequency of light in the medium divided by its frequency in a vacuum; always greater than 1
questions.explanation: The absolute refractive index is n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in the medium. Because light always slows when it enters a medium, v is less than c, so the refractive index is always larger than 1 (water 1.33, glass about 1.5, diamond 2.42).

questions.q: When light travels from a medium of lower refractive index into a medium of higher refractive index, how is the ray bent at the boundary?
options: It is bent away from the normal, so that r > i
It is bent towards the normal, so that r < i (if n2 > n1)
It continues in a straight line without bending
It is reflected back along the incident ray
questions.explanation: If light travels from a lower refractive index medium to a medium with a higher refractive index it bends towards the normal: if n2 > n1 then r < i. The ray slows on entering the optically denser medium, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence.

questions.q: A ray of light in air strikes a glass block of refractive index 1.45 at an angle of incidence of 30°. Using Snell's Law, calculate the angle of refraction in the glass.
questions.explanation: Substitute into Snell's Law n1 sin i = n2 sin r, divide both sides by 1.45 to isolate sin r, then take the inverse sine. The refracted angle (20°) is smaller than the incident angle (30°) because the ray entered a denser, higher-index medium and bent towards the normal.

questions.q: In Snell's Law, n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r), what do the symbols n1 and i represent?
options: n1 is the refractive index of the new medium and i is the angle of refraction
n1 is the refractive index of the incident medium and i is the incident angle
n1 is the critical angle and i is the speed of light in medium 1
n1 is the angle of incidence and i is the refractive index of medium 1
questions.explanation: Snell's Law, first formulated around 1621 by Willebrord Snell, is n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r), where n1 is the refractive index of the incident medium and i is the incident angle, while n2 is the refractive index of the new medium and r is the angle of refraction.

questions.q: Calculate the critical angle for light rays passing from water (refractive index 1.3) into air.
questions.given: n_water = 1.3,  n_air = 1.0,  refracted angle = 90° at the critical angle
questions.explanation: The critical angle is found from Snell's Law by setting the angle of refraction to its maximum value of 90°, so sin(ic) = n2/n1. For water into air this gives sin(ic) = 1.0/1.3 = 0.7692, hence about 50°. Beyond this angle total internal reflection occurs.

questions.q: When white light passes through a triangular glass prism and disperses into a spectrum, which colour is refracted the most and why?
options: Red light, because it travels the slowest through the glass
Violet light, because it travels the slowest through the glass and has the highest refractive index
All colours are refracted equally because they share the same refractive index
Green light, because it lies in the middle of the visible spectrum
questions.explanation: Dispersion occurs because the different colours of the visible spectrum travel through the glass at different velocities, so each colour has a slightly different refractive index. Violet light, which travels the slowest, is refracted the most, while red light, which travels the fastest, is refracted the least.

questions.q: From memory: state the two conditions that must both be met for total internal reflection to occur, and what happens to the light when they are met.
keyPoints: The light must travel from a medium of higher refractive index towards a medium of lower refractive index (denser to less dense, n1 > n2).
The angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle.
When both hold, all the light is reflected back into the original medium and no refracted ray is formed.
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection needs both conditions: higher-index to lower-index travel AND an incident angle greater than the critical angle. If you recalled both conditions plus that all the light is reflected back into the original medium (used technologically in optical fibres), grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: According to the ray model summary, which statement correctly pairs a model feature with its rule?
options: The ray model depicts light as straight lines, and the Law of Reflection states the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The ray model depicts light as expanding spheres, and reflection reverses the frequency of the wave
The ray model depicts light as straight lines, and the absolute refractive index of any medium is always less than 1
The Law of Reflection states the incident ray and reflected ray lie in perpendicular planes
questions.explanation: The ray model depicts light as straight lines in a uniform medium, with all angles measured from the normal. The Law of Reflection states that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane.

questions.q: A light meter reads 200 lux at 1 m from a small lamp. Using the inverse-square law for light intensity, what will it read at 4 m from the lamp?
questions.explanation: Light from a point source spreads over an expanding sphere, so intensity follows the inverse square of distance: I1 r1² = I2 r2². Four times the distance gives one sixteenth the intensity, so 200 lux drops to 12.5 lux. The classic trap is forgetting to square the distance ratio (it is 16, not 4).

questions.q: From memory: explain how an optical fibre uses total internal reflection to carry light along its length, and give one practical use.
keyPoints: An optical fibre is a thin glass thread of high refractive index; light enters one end and strikes the internal walls at angles of incidence greater than the critical angle.

Because the light travels from the dense glass towards the less dense surroundings, it totally internally reflects at each wall, bouncing repeatedly down the fibre with almost no loss, even around bends.
Uses: carrying internet and telephone data as pulses of light over long distances, or carrying images out of the body in a medical endoscope.
questions.explanation: The fibre meets both TIR conditions at every wall (dense-to-less-dense travel and angle above the critical angle), so the signal travels efficiently end to end. If you recalled the repeated reflection above the critical angle plus a valid use, grade yourself Good or Easy.
